title: The year of the Elephant
notes: The Quran says only that God dealt with "the People of the Elephant" by sending flocks of birds that pelted them with stones. Tradition tells of an army led by Abraha, the Abyssinian ruler of Yemen, which marched on Mecca with an elephant and was destroyed, and says Muhammad was born in that year. The date of about 570 is traditional and uncertain.

title: The years at Mecca
notes: From the first revelation to the move to Medina. Muhammad preaches in his own city to a small following, against the opposition of its leaders. By the traditional count, 86 of the 114 surahs belong to these years: most of the short surahs, and the long retellings of the earlier prophets.

title: The first revelation
notes: Tradition says that the first words came to Muhammad at the age of about forty, in a cave on Mount Hira outside Mecca, brought by the angel Gabriel: "Read: In the Name of your Lord who created" (96:1-5). The Quran says it was sent down on the Night of Decree (97:1), in the month of Ramadan (2:185); it does not describe the occasion.

title: The call to warn openly
notes: "Arise and warn" (74:2); "warn your close relatives" (26:214); "proclaim openly what you are commanded" (15:94). Tradition says that after a first period of private preaching Muhammad was told to preach in public, about three years after the first revelation.

title: The Romans are defeated
notes: "The Romans have been defeated in a nearby territory. But following their defeat, they will be victorious in a few years." The Persians took Syria and Jerusalem from the Byzantines in 613 and 614; the emperor Heraclius defeated them in the 620s. This is the one event of the wider world of its day that the Quran mentions.

title: Some believers take refuge in Abyssinia
notes: Tradition says that a group of Muhammad's followers, persecuted at Mecca, crossed the sea to the Christian king of Abyssinia. The Quran does not mention it; some commentators connect it with the promise to "those who emigrate for God's sake after being persecuted" (16:41).

title: The night journey
notes: "Glory to Him who journeyed His servant by night, from the Sacred Mosque, to the Farthest Mosque" (17:1). That verse is all the Quran says of the journey. Tradition tells of a journey to Jerusalem in one night and an ascent from there through the heavens, and reads the vision "at the Lotus Tree of the Extremity" (53:13-18) as part of it. The date is traditional.

title: The years at Medina
notes: From the move to Medina to Muhammad's death. He now leads a community, and the surahs of these years (28 by the traditional count, and the longest) turn to law, to war and treaties with Mecca, and to the Jews, the Christians and the "hypocrites" of Medina.

title: The move to Medina (the Hijra)
notes: Muhammad and his followers leave Mecca for Yathrib, afterward called Medina: the event from which the Muslim calendar is counted. The Quran recalls that the unbelievers plotted "to imprison you, or kill you, or expel you" (8:30), and that he was "the second of two in the cave", saying to his friend, "Do not worry, God is with us" (9:40). By tradition the friend was Abu Bakr, and the cave was on Mount Thawr near Mecca.

title: The direction of prayer is changed
notes: "Turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque" (2:144). The passage says that the earlier direction was a test, and that "the ignorant among the people" will ask why it changed. Tradition says the believers had prayed toward Jerusalem until then; the Quran does not name the earlier direction.

title: The battle of Badr
notes: "God had given you victory at Badr, when you were weak" (3:123): the one battle with Mecca that the Quran names. Surah 8 speaks of "the Day of Distinction, the day when the two armies met" (8:41), of angels sent to help, and of the spoils. Tradition says some three hundred Muslims defeated a Meccan force three times their number.

title: The battle of Uhud
notes: The Quran does not name the battle. It speaks of a morning when the Prophet set the believers in their positions (3:121), of a victory that turned into a setback when some "disputed the command" (3:152), of the believers fleeing while the Messenger called to them (3:153), and of the rumor of his death: "Muhammad is no more than a messenger" (3:144). Tradition places this at Mount Uhud, outside Medina.

title: A tribe of the People of the Book is driven out
notes: "It is He who evicted those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first mobilization" (59:2); they thought their fortresses would protect them. Tradition identifies them as the Banu Nadir, a Jewish tribe of Medina, exiled after being accused of plotting against Muhammad. The Quran does not name the tribe.

title: The siege of Medina (the Trench)
notes: "Forces came against you", from above and below; the hypocrites said "O people of Yathrib, you cannot make a stand"; and God sent against the confederates "a wind, and forces you did not see" (33:9-13). The Quran does not mention a trench. Tradition tells of an alliance of Mecca and other tribes besieging Medina, held off by a ditch dug around the town.

title: Those who backed the confederates are brought down
notes: "He brought down from their strongholds those of the People of the Book who backed them, and He threw terror into their hearts. Some of them you killed, and others you took captive" (33:26). Tradition identifies them as the Banu Qurayza, a Jewish tribe of Medina, and says that their men were put to death and their women and children enslaved. The Quran gives no name and no number.

title: The slander
notes: "Those who perpetrated the slander are a band of you" (24:11); the believers are rebuked for repeating it without four witnesses. Tradition says the accusation was made against Aisha, the Prophet's wife, after she was left behind by a caravan. The Quran does not name her.

title: The Prophet marries the former wife of Zayd
notes: "When Zaid ended his relationship with her, We gave her to you in marriage, that there may be no restriction for believers regarding the wives of their adopted sons" (33:37). Tradition names her as Zaynab bint Jahsh, a cousin of Muhammad, who had been married to his adopted son Zayd. The same passage declares that Muhammad "is not the father of any of your men" (33:40).

title: The pledge under the tree, and the truce
notes: "God was pleased with the believers, when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree" (48:18); He "withheld their hands from you, and your hands from them, in the valley of Mecca" (48:24), after the unbelievers "barred you from the Sacred Mosque" (48:25). Tradition tells of a journey to make the pilgrimage that was stopped at Hudaybiyya, outside Mecca, and ended in a ten-year truce; the surah calls it "a conspicuous victory". The Quran does not name the place.

title: Mecca is taken
notes: "When there comes God's victory, and conquest, and you see the people entering God's religion in multitudes" (110:1-2). The Quran speaks of "the conquest" as a dividing line between earlier and later believers (57:10) but does not describe it. Tradition says that Muhammad entered Mecca with little fighting after the truce was broken, and cleared the Kaaba of its idols.

title: The battle of Hunayn
notes: "On the day of Hunayn, your great number impressed you, but it availed you nothing; and the land, as spacious as it was, narrowed for you; and you turned your backs in retreat. Then God sent down His serenity" (9:25-26). Tradition places the battle shortly after the taking of Mecca, against tribes to its east.

title: The expedition many would not join
notes: "What is the matter with you, when it is said to you, Mobilize in the cause of God, you cling heavily to the earth?" (9:38). Much of surah 9 concerns a distant march in the heat, those who asked to be excused, and "the three who were left behind" and were forgiven (9:118). Tradition identifies it as the expedition to Tabuk, toward the Byzantine frontier. The Quran does not name the place.

title: The treaties with the idolaters are ended
notes: "A proclamation from God and His Messenger to the people on the day of the Greater Pilgrimage, that God has disowned the polytheists" (9:3): four months' notice, after which those who had broken their treaties were to be fought unless they repented; and "let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs" (9:28). Tradition says the proclamation was read out at the pilgrimage of 631.

title: The farewell pilgrimage
notes: "Today I have perfected your religion for you, and have completed My favor upon you, and have approved Islam as a religion for you" (5:3). Tradition says these words were revealed at Arafat during Muhammad's last pilgrimage, a few months before his death.

title: The death of Muhammad
notes: The Quran does not record it. It had said, "Muhammad is no more than a messenger. Messengers have passed on before him. If he dies or gets killed, will you turn on your heels?" (3:144), and "You will die, and they will die" (39:30). Tradition says he died at Medina in June 632, and that the first of these verses was recited to the people that day.
